groups.high: Basel III distinguishes minimum capital requirements from additional buffers. The baseline Common Equity Tier 1, or CET1, minimum is 4.5% of risk-weighted assets. A 2.5% capital conservation buffer is also met with CET1, producing 7% when those two requirements are combined. Tier 1 includes CET1 and qualifying Additional Tier 1 instruments; total capital adds qualifying Tier 2. Baseline minima are 6% for Tier 1 and 8% for total capital before buffers. Risk-weighted assets reflect credit, market, and operational risk under specified rules, not simply the cash value of loans. Entering the conservation buffer restricts distributions such as dividends according to the framework; it is not identical to breaching the 4.5% minimum. Countercyclical, systemic-bank, and supervisory requirements can add further capital. The baseline leverage ratio is 3% Tier 1 capital relative to its defined exposure measure, which includes specified off-balance-sheet items, not just unweighted balance-sheet assets. Basel standards require implementation through domestic rules and do not guarantee that a compliant bank cannot fail. Capital absorbs losses; liquidity addresses the ability to meet payments, a related but distinct issue.
groups.mid: Basel III asks banks to hold capital to absorb losses. Its basic Common Equity Tier 1, or CET1, minimum is 4.5% of risk-weighted assets. A further 2.5% conservation buffer must also be CET1. Together, these make 7%. Tier 1 includes CET1 and qualifying Additional Tier 1 instruments. Total capital adds qualifying Tier 2. Before buffers, the basic minimum is 6% for Tier 1 and 8% for total capital. Risk-weighted assets measure credit, market, and operational risks under set rules. They are not simply the face value of loans. If a bank uses its conservation buffer, rules limit payouts such as dividends. This is different from falling below the 4.5% minimum. Extra rules for credit cycles, major banks, or supervision can require more capital. The basic leverage ratio is 3% Tier 1 capital divided by a defined exposure measure. That measure includes some items outside the balance sheet, not just ordinary assets. Countries put Basel standards into their own laws. Meeting them does not promise a bank can never fail. Capital cushions losses; liquidity means having funds to meet payments. Both matter, but they are different.
groups.low: Banks need capital to absorb losses. Basel III sets a basic rule for Common Equity Tier 1, or CET1. It must be at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets. There is a further 2.5% conservation buffer in CET1. Together, these make 7%. Tier 1 includes CET1 and qualifying Additional Tier 1. Add qualifying Tier 2 to get total capital. Before buffers, the basic minimum is 6% for Tier 1 and 8% for total capital. Risk-weighted assets count credit, market, and operational risk under set rules. They are not just the money value of loans. If a bank uses the buffer, rules limit payouts such as dividends. This is not the same as going below the 4.5% minimum. Other rules may require more for credit cycles, large banks, or local supervision. The basic leverage ratio is 3%. It compares Tier 1 with a defined exposure measure. Some items outside the balance sheet count too. It is not just a total of ordinary assets. Each country puts Basel rules into its own system. A bank can still fail while meeting a rule. Capital covers losses. Liquidity helps meet payments when due. They are linked, but not the same.
groups.source_review: Checked BIS minimum ratios, buffers, distribution constraints, and leverage denominator.
groups.notes: Corrected automatic sanction characterization, missing Tier 1 minimum, and on-balance-sheet-only leverage definition.

groups.high: Under US securities law, unlawful insider trading generally involves trading on material nonpublic information in breach of a duty of trust or confidence, or other applicable deceptive conduct. Material information would matter to a reasonable investor; nonpublic information has not been adequately disseminated. Corporate insiders are not prohibited from every trade, and mere receipt of confidential information does not automatically establish every element of a crime. Tipping and trading by recipients can also create liability depending on the facts and legal requirements. Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act 1934 and Rule 10b-5 are central provisions. Under 15 USC 78ff, covered willful violations can carry up to twenty years' imprisonment and a statutory individual fine of $5 million, with other fine provisions potentially relevant. These are maxima, not automatic sentences. Civil insider-trading penalties can be tied to up to three times profit gained or loss avoided, alongside disgorgement and other remedies; a universal $10 million civil cap is incorrect. The 1984 Insider Trading Sanctions Act expanded civil enforcement, not a blanket criminal ban on possessing information. Seek compliance or legal guidance before trading or sharing potentially sensitive information.
groups.mid: US law generally bans trading on an important secret if it breaks a duty of trust or involves unlawful deceit. The legal term is material nonpublic information. Material means a reasonable investor would think it matters. Nonpublic means it has not been properly shared with the public. Company insiders can make lawful trades. Getting a secret does not prove every part of a crime. Giving a tip or using one can also lead to liability. The facts and legal tests matter. Key rules include section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act 1934 and Rule 10b-5. Under 15 USC 78ff, some willful breaches can bring up to twenty years in prison. A person can face a statutory $5 million fine. Other fine rules may apply. These are maximums, not fixed sentences. Civil insider-trading penalties can reach three times the profit made or loss avoided. A court can order gains repaid and other remedies too. There is no single $10 million civil cap for all cases. The 1984 Insider Trading Sanctions Act strengthened civil enforcement. It did not make just holding a secret a crime. Get compliance or legal advice before trading or sharing sensitive information.
groups.low: US law can ban trading on an important secret when it breaks a duty of trust or uses unlawful deceit. This is material nonpublic information. Material means it matters to a reasonable investor. Nonpublic means it has not been properly shared with all. An insider can still make a lawful trade. Just getting a secret does not prove a crime. Giving a tip or using it to trade can also cause legal trouble. Facts and legal tests matter. Key rules are section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act 1934 and Rule 10b-5. Under 15 USC 78ff, some willful breaches can bring up to twenty years in jail. A person can face a statutory $5 million fine. Other fine rules may apply. These are maximums, not fixed punishments. A civil insider-trading penalty can reach three times the profit made or loss avoided. A court may order gains repaid and other steps. There is no single $10 million civil cap. The 1984 Insider Trading Sanctions Act strengthened civil enforcement. It did not ban just holding a secret. Ask a legal or compliance adviser before you trade or share sensitive news.
groups.source_review: Checked official statute and DOJ maximum-penalty example; SEC-hosted issuer policy used only as supplemental summary of three-times civil penalty.
groups.notes: Corrected overbroad possession liability, invented civil cap, and 1984 Act characterization.

groups.high: Deposit insurance protects eligible deposits when an insured bank fails, subject to coverage rules and limits. US FDIC coverage is generally $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Multiple accounts in the same category at one bank are combined; opening another account or using another branch does not automatically add coverage. Distinct qualifying ownership categories can be insured separately. Checking and savings accounts and certificates of deposit can qualify; stocks, mutual funds, cryptoassets, and other non-deposit investments are not FDIC-insured merely because sold through a bank. EU Directive 2014/49/EU establishes standard protection of €100,000 per depositor per bank through national deposit guarantee schemes, with specified special treatment such as qualifying temporary high balances. It is not an unrestricted choice for each country to set ordinary coverage as high as it likes. Coverage depends on institution, eligibility, aggregation, and applicable rules. Insurance supports confidence and can reduce runs, but does not eliminate all bank risk or reimburse every uninsured asset. Confirm the actual insured bank and account ownership, particularly for intermediated products, and use official coverage tools before assuming the full balance is protected.
groups.mid: Deposit insurance covers eligible bank money if an insured bank fails. US FDIC cover is generally $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Accounts in the same category at one bank are added together. Another account or branch does not automatically add cover. A different qualifying ownership category may have separate cover. Checking, savings, and certificates of deposit can qualify. Stocks, mutual funds, cryptoassets, and other investments do not gain FDIC cover just because a bank sells them. EU Directive 2014/49/EU gives standard cover of €100,000 per depositor per bank. National schemes provide it. Some temporary high balances have special rules. Countries cannot just choose any ordinary limit they want. The bank, type of money held, ownership, and rules for adding accounts all matter. Insurance builds trust and can reduce bank runs. It cannot remove all bank risk. It does not cover every asset. Check which bank actually holds the money. This matters if a platform or another firm is involved. Use official coverage tools. Do not assume the full balance is insured.
groups.low: Deposit insurance can protect eligible bank deposits if the bank fails. The US FDIC generally covers $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Accounts in the same category at one bank are added together. A new account or another branch does not always add cover. A different qualifying ownership category can have separate cover. Checking accounts, savings, and certificates of deposit can qualify. Stocks, mutual funds, cryptoassets, and other investments do not get FDIC cover. A bank selling them does not change this. EU Directive 2014/49/EU gives standard cover of €100,000 per depositor per bank through national schemes. Some temporary high balances have special rules. Countries cannot just choose any normal limit they want. Check the bank, type of deposit, ownership, and rules for adding accounts together. Insurance helps build trust and reduce bank runs. It does not remove all bank risk or protect every asset. If a platform or other firm stands between you and the bank, find out which bank holds the money. Use official coverage tools. Do not assume your whole balance is covered.
groups.source_review: Checked FDIC ownership aggregation, product exclusions, and EU standard limit; special balances left subject to applicable national/implementation rules.
groups.notes: Corrected arbitrary national higher-limit claim and guarantee that insurance eliminates bank runs.

groups.high: US currency and suspicious-activity reporting are distinct obligations. A Currency Transaction Report generally applies to cash transactions totaling more than $10,000 in a business day, subject to relevant aggregation and exemptions. It is not automatically triggered by exactly $10,000 or every electronic transfer. Known transactions by or on behalf of one person may need aggregation. Deliberately structuring transactions to evade reporting can be unlawful even when the money itself is legitimate. A report is not proof that a customer committed money laundering. Suspicious Activity Report requirements depend on institution type, conduct, amount, and other rules. US bank rules include different triggers, such as insider abuse involving any amount and certain suspicious transactions aggregating at least $5,000; voluntary reporting can be possible below mandatory thresholds. FATF Recommendation 20's general suspicion standard should not be substituted for every domestic filing rule. Institutions also have confidentiality obligations concerning SARs. Customers should provide accurate information and must not split transactions to avoid reporting. Compliance staff should consult the current applicable rules rather than rely on a single 'AML threshold' or assume that lower amounts are unmonitored.
groups.mid: US cash reports and suspicious-activity reports differ. A Currency Transaction Report is called a CTR. It generally applies when cash totals more than $10,000 in a business day. Rules may add related sums together or allow exemptions. Exactly $10,000 is not more than $10,000. An electronic transfer is not always cash. A bank may combine known transactions made by or for one person. Splitting them to evade reporting can be illegal, even if the money is legal. A report does not prove money laundering. A Suspicious Activity Report, or SAR, has different triggers. The type of firm and the conduct matter. US bank rules may require a report of insider abuse at any amount. Some suspicious transactions adding up to at least $5,000 must be reported. Voluntary reports may be allowed below the mandatory limit. FATF Recommendation 20 gives a general standard. It is not each country's detailed filing rule. SARs have secrecy rules too. Give accurate details and do not split sums to evade reporting. Compliance staff must check current rules. There is no single AML amount below which nothing is monitored.
groups.low: US cash reports and suspicious-activity reports differ. A cash report is called a CTR. It generally applies when cash totals more than $10,000 in one business day. Rules may add related transactions together or allow exemptions. Exactly $10,000 is not more than $10,000. An electronic transfer is not always cash. A bank may combine known transactions made by or for one person. Do not split them to avoid a report. This can be illegal even if the money is legal. A report does not prove money laundering. A suspicious-activity report is called a SAR. Its rules depend on the type of firm and what happened. US bank rules have different triggers. Insider abuse may count at any amount. Some suspicious transactions adding up to at least $5,000 must be reported. A firm may also report below a required limit. FATF Recommendation 20 is a general standard. It is not every local filing rule. SARs have secrecy rules too. Give honest details and do not split sums to evade reporting. Compliance staff must check current rules. There is no single AML amount below which nothing is checked.
groups.source_review: Checked FinCEN CTR aggregation and SAR filing categories; no evasion tactics supplied.
groups.notes: Corrected over-versus-at-least threshold, erroneous regulation citation, and universal zero-threshold mandatory SAR claim.

groups.high: For unauthorized use of a US credit card, TILA and Regulation Z generally limit a cardholder's liability to no more than $50, subject to statutory conditions. If loss or theft is reported before unauthorized use, the cardholder is not responsible for subsequent unauthorized charges. If only the account number is stolen and the physical card remains with the holder, CFPB guidance states there is no liability for unauthorized charges. Many issuers offer broader zero-liability policies, but eligibility and procedures should be checked rather than assumed. Credit-card protections differ from debit-card and bank-transfer rules, where reporting delays can have different consequences. Promptly contact the issuer through a trusted number or application, secure or replace the card as directed, and retain the report confirmation. Review statements and dispute errors in writing when required. A formal billing-error notice generally has a sixty-day deadline from the statement containing the error, a separate issue from the unauthorized-use liability ceiling. Do not wait merely because the possible liability seems small. The protections concern unauthorized transactions, not every purchase dispute or charge the cardholder later regrets.
groups.mid: US credit-card law generally limits what you owe for unauthorized use to $50, under TILA and Regulation Z and their conditions. If you report a lost or stolen card before someone uses it, you do not owe for later unauthorized charges. If only the card number is stolen and you still have the card, CFPB says you are not liable for those unauthorized charges. Many issuers offer zero liability, but check the policy and reporting steps. Credit cards are not the same as debit cards or bank transfers. Delays can have different effects under those rules. Call the issuer through a trusted number or app as soon as you spot the problem. Secure or replace the card as advised, and keep the report confirmation. Check statements and send a written dispute if required. A formal billing-error notice generally must arrive within sixty days of the statement showing the error. That deadline is separate from the $50 liability ceiling. Do not wait because the possible loss looks small. These rules cover unauthorized use, not every purchase you dispute or later regret.
groups.low: For a US credit card, you generally owe no more than $50 for unauthorized use. TILA and Regulation Z set conditions. If you report the card lost or stolen before it is used, you do not owe for later unauthorized charges. If only the number is stolen and you still have the card, CFPB says you do not owe for those charges. Many card firms offer zero liability. Check the policy and its reporting steps. Debit cards and bank transfers have different rules. Waiting can have different costs. Call the card firm through a trusted number or app as soon as you see a problem. Lock or replace the card as advised. Keep proof of the report and check your statements. Send a written dispute when needed. A formal billing-error notice generally has a sixty-day limit from the statement with the error. This is a different issue from the $50 cap. Do not delay just because the possible cost seems small. The rules cover unauthorized use. They do not cover every purchase you dislike or regret.
groups.source_review: Checked CFPB credit-card-specific liability and billing-dispute guidance; distinguished debit rules.
groups.notes: Added number-only theft protection and distinction between report procedures, zero-liability policies, and billing-error deadlines.

groups.high: TRIPS Article 33 requires available patent protection not to end before twenty years from the patent application's filing date. This is an international minimum term, not a worldwide patent or an unconditional twenty-year guarantee for every right. Domestic rules determine the relevant filing date, maintenance fees, adjustments or extensions, and possible earlier revocation or lapse. Foreign priority does not automatically make the earliest worldwide filing the term's starting date; the precise application chain matters. A patent generally permits exclusion of others from covered acts within its territory, not an affirmative clearance to practice every aspect of the invention. The Patent Law Treaty harmonizes formal procedures; it does not create mutual recognition of all patents or establish a uniform substantive patent term. Patent disclosure is generally published before expiry, not kept legally secret until it 'reverts' then. After expiry, the expired claims no longer exclude others, but other patents, regulatory requirements, or rights can still constrain a product. Check the patent register, claim scope, status, jurisdiction, and dates before assuming freedom to operate. Design rights and utility models can have different terms.
groups.mid: TRIPS Article 33 says available patent protection must not end before twenty years from the application's filing date. This is a minimum standard, not one world patent or a promise that every patent lasts exactly twenty years. Local rules decide which filing date counts, fees, extensions, and reasons a patent may end early. The first filing anywhere in the world is not always the start date. The chain of applications matters. A patent lets the owner stop certain acts covered by its claims in that territory. It does not automatically give permission to make or sell the whole product. The Patent Law Treaty deals with formal procedures. It does not make all countries recognize each other's patents or set one term for all rights. Patent details are usually published before expiry. They do not stay secret until the term ends. Once claims expire, those claims no longer block use. Other patents, rules, or rights may still apply. Before making a product, check the register, claims, status, country, and dates. Design rights and utility models may have different terms.
groups.low: TRIPS Article 33 sets a patent-term rule. Available protection must not end before twenty years from the application's filing date. This is a minimum standard, not one patent for the whole world. It is not a promise that every patent lasts exactly twenty years. Local rules decide which filing date counts. Fees, extensions, cancellation, or lapse can change the end date. The first filing in the world is not always the start date. Check the linked applications. A patent lets its owner stop certain acts covered by its claims in that country. It does not clear every part of a product for sale. The Patent Law Treaty makes formal steps more alike. It does not make all patents valid in all countries or set every term. Patent details are usually made public before expiry. When claims expire, they no longer block use. Other patents, rules, or rights may still block a product. Check the register, claims, status, place, and dates before you act. Design rights and utility models can have different terms.
groups.source_review: Checked TRIPS minimum, WIPO PLT scope, and USPTO filing-chain/foreign-priority distinction.
groups.notes: Corrected earliest-worldwide filing, invented Latin doctrine, mutual recognition, and post-expiry administrative-right claims.

groups.high: US fair use under 17 USC 107 permits some uses of copyrighted expression without permission, assessed case by case. Criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, and research are examples, not automatic exemptions. Courts consider the purpose and character of the use, including commercial or nonprofit educational context; the nature of the copyrighted work; the amount and qualitative importance taken; and effects on the work's potential market or value. New meaning alone does not automatically make a use fair; purpose and context still matter. Factual works may favor fair use more than highly creative ones, while unpublished status can weigh against it but does not itself bar a finding. A short excerpt can take the heart of a work, and an entire work can sometimes be justified by a particular purpose. There is no universal safe word count or percentage. Credit is good practice but does not replace permission or establish fair use. Balance all factors in the actual circumstances and consider licensing or qualified legal advice for substantial risk. Other jurisdictions use different exceptions, so US fair use cannot be assumed worldwide.
groups.mid: US fair use, in 17 USC 107, can allow some use of copyrighted work without permission. It depends on the case. Criticism, comment, news, teaching, scholarship, and research may qualify, but their labels are not automatic passes. Courts weigh four things: why and how you use the work; the kind of work; how much and how important a part you take; and the effect on its market or value. Commercial and nonprofit teaching uses can weigh differently. Adding a new meaning alone does not settle the question. Facts may favor fair use more than creative work. Unpublished work may weigh against it, but can still qualify. A small quote may take the most important part. A whole work may sometimes be needed for a valid purpose. There is no fixed safe word count or percentage. Giving credit is good, but does not itself give permission or make use fair. Weigh the facts together. Consider a license or legal advice if the risk is high. Other countries have different exceptions, so do not assume US fair use applies everywhere.
groups.low: US law sometimes lets you use copyrighted work without asking. This is fair use under 17 USC 107. It depends on the facts. Criticism, comment, news, teaching, scholarship, or research may qualify. Just using one of those labels is not enough. A court weighs four things. Why and how do you use it? What kind of work is it? How much do you take, and is it a key part? What effect could it have on the work's market or value? Commercial use and nonprofit teaching may weigh differently. A new meaning alone does not prove fair use. Factual work may be easier to use fairly than highly creative work. Unpublished work may weigh against fair use, but is not always barred. A short quote can take the heart of a work. In some cases, a whole work is needed. There is no safe word count or percentage for all uses. Give credit, but know that credit alone is not permission or fair use. Weigh all the facts. A license or legal advice may help with risk. Other countries have different exceptions. US fair use is not a world rule.
groups.source_review: Checked Copyright Office guidance and statutory four factors, including unpublished-work proviso.
groups.notes: Corrected reversed unpublished-work treatment and automatic transformative/educational assumptions.

groups.high: Confidential source protection supports investigative journalism by reducing the risk that potential informants will be exposed or deterred. In the European Convention system, Article 10 protects freedom of expression, and Goodwin v United Kingdom emphasizes that compelled source disclosure requires an overriding public-interest justification. This is strong but qualified protection, not an absolute guarantee or a uniform rule in every democracy. Restrictions must satisfy applicable legality, legitimate-aim, necessity, and proportionality requirements. Sanoma Uitgevers v Netherlands also emphasizes effective independent review of source-identifying disclosure. Protection can concern information or materials that identify a source indirectly, not only a name. National shield laws, court procedures, exceptions, and who qualifies vary. A general invocation of national security or an official desire for information does not automatically settle the balance. UNESCO media indicators assess protections but do not themselves create a global legal privilege. Journalists should assess legal and digital risks, limit unnecessary identifying data, explain limits honestly to sources, and obtain specialist advice promptly if compelled disclosure is threatened. Do not promise confidentiality that the law or technical arrangements cannot reliably provide.
groups.mid: A confidential source may give a journalist facts without wanting to be named. Protecting that source helps the press inform the public. Fear of being exposed can stop people speaking. In the European Convention system, Article 10 protects free expression. Goodwin v United Kingdom says forced source disclosure needs an overriding public-interest reason. The protection is strong, but not absolute. It is not one rule for every democracy. A restriction needs a legal basis and proper aim. It must also be necessary and proportionate. Sanoma Uitgevers v Netherlands stresses independent review of demands for source-identifying material. A name is not the only risk. Notes or data can expose a source too. Each country's shield laws, court steps, exceptions, and protected people can differ. Officials cannot just invoke national security and assume protection is lost. UNESCO media indicators assess safeguards. They do not create a world legal privilege. Check legal and digital risks. Keep no needless identifying data. Explain limits honestly to sources. Get specialist advice quickly if disclosure is demanded. Do not promise secrecy that the law or technology cannot provide.
groups.low: A source may give facts to a journalist in confidence. They do not want to be named. Keeping that source safe helps the press inform the public. Fear of being exposed can stop people speaking. Article 10 of the European Convention protects free expression. The Goodwin case says there must be a very strong public-interest reason to force a source to be named. Protection is strong, but not absolute. It is not the same in every democracy. A limit must be based on law and have a proper aim. It must be needed and no more than needed too. The Sanoma case calls for a review by someone independent. This should happen before handing over material that could reveal a source. Notes and data can reveal a source, not just a name. Local shield laws differ. So do court steps, exceptions, and who has protection. Officials cannot just say national security. That alone does not settle the issue. UNESCO media indicators measure safeguards. They do not make a world legal privilege. Check risks in law and digital tools. Keep no needless data that could name a source. Explain the limits honestly. Get expert help quickly if officials demand names or notes. Do not promise secrecy that law or digital tools cannot protect.
groups.source_review: Checked ECtHR Goodwin, Sanoma, and source-protection factsheet; territorial framework explicit.
groups.notes: Removed blanket constitutional/global guarantee and automatic exception examples; added independent review and indirect identification.

groups.high: A trademark identifies commercial source rather than the generic category of goods or services. Genericide occurs when the relevant public primarily understands a formerly distinctive mark as the category name. US 15 USC 1064(3) permits cancellation on this ground, judged by the mark's primary significance to the relevant public. Mere popularity or occasional noun or verb use is not necessarily decisive. Descriptive terms and generic terms are different: acquired distinctiveness may protect some descriptive terms, but a generic name cannot be monopolized for its category. Consumer association with a single source can support distinctiveness, not automatically cause genericity. Historical examples such as aspirin and escalator must be interpreted by jurisdiction and period; a word may remain a trademark elsewhere. Owners can promote consistent brand-plus-product wording, explain correct usage, and monitor relevant public understanding. Enforcement cannot guarantee protection if the term has become generic, and competitors' legitimate use of category names must be respected. Trademark rights are territorial and goods-specific; the status of Kleenex or any other current brand should not be guessed. Legal assessment requires evidence of consumer meaning, not a list of famous brand names alone.
groups.mid: A trademark tells customers which business supplies a product. It is different from the name of the product category. Genericide happens when people mainly understand an old brand name as the category itself. Under US 15 USC 1064(3), registration can be cancelled for that reason. The key is what the name mainly means to the relevant public. A popular brand, or a word sometimes used as a noun or verb, does not automatically fail. A descriptive name and a generic name are different. Some descriptive names gain protection when people learn the source. A generic category name cannot be owned for that category. Being linked with one business can help distinctiveness, not automatically destroy it. Aspirin and escalator are historical examples, but country and date matter. A name may still be protected elsewhere. Owners can use a brand with the product name, explain proper use, and track public meaning. Legal action cannot promise success once a name is generic. Respect competitors' right to name the category. Rights depend on country and goods. Do not guess the current status of Kleenex or another brand. Consumer evidence is needed.
groups.low: A trademark shows which business a product comes from, not the name for the whole type of product. Genericide means people mainly treat an old brand as the type's name. US 15 USC 1064(3) lets a registration be cancelled for this. What the relevant public understands the word to mean is key. A famous brand is not automatically generic, nor is a word just because some people use it as a noun or verb. A descriptive term and a generic name differ. Some descriptive terms gain protection when people learn the source. No one can own the generic name for its whole category. A link with one business may help a brand stay distinct. Aspirin and escalator are past examples, but the place and date matter. A word may still be a brand elsewhere. Owners can put the brand beside the product name, explain correct use, and track public meaning. Legal action cannot always save a generic name. Other firms may use a real category name. Rights depend on country and goods, so do not guess if Kleenex or another brand has lost rights. Check evidence of what consumers mean.
groups.source_review: Checked statutory primary-significance test and USPTO descriptive/generic distinctions. Historical examples qualified; unsupported current brand-status claims removed.
groups.notes: Corrected reversed acquired-distinctiveness reasoning and invented cross-country brand-loss claims.

groups.high: A right of reply is a jurisdiction-specific opportunity to respond to a publication; it is not identical to a defamation claim or an automatic worldwide entitlement to equal space. France's Law of 29 July 1881 on freedom of the press contains a reply mechanism in Article 13 for people named or designated in qualifying periodical publications. Its operation depends on statutory requirements, including the publication format, request, timing, content, and length. The claimant need not simply assume that only proven defamation creates a right, or that a reply can include any allegation. Different provisions govern online communication and other media. Comparable placement and type may be required under the applicable French provision, but this must not be generalized to every jurisdiction or every outlet. Preserve the publication, date, exact reference, proposed reply, and proof of delivery, and obtain advice quickly because deadlines can be short. An editorial correction, a legal reply, and a damages action serve different purposes and may follow separate procedures. UNESCO or broad press-freedom principles do not substitute for the governing domestic rule. Whether refusal is unlawful and what remedy follows requires the current text and facts.
groups.mid: A right of reply lets someone respond to a publication under a particular law. It is not the same as a defamation claim, and it is not a world rule giving equal space in every outlet. France's Law of 29 July 1881 on press freedom has a reply rule in Article 13. It covers people named or identified in certain periodicals. The format, request, deadlines, content, and length all matter. Do not assume you must first prove defamation. Do not assume the reply may say anything either. Online and other media can have different rules. French law may require comparable placement and type, but this does not apply automatically to every country or outlet. Keep the article, date, exact mention, draft reply, and proof that your request arrived. Get advice quickly, since time limits can be short. An editor's correction, a legal reply, and a claim for damages are different steps. Broad press-freedom principles or UNESCO guidance do not replace the local law. Check the current text and facts. A refusal is not always illegal, and a remedy is not guaranteed.
groups.low: Some laws let you reply when an article names or identifies you. This is a right of reply. It is not the same as suing for defamation. It is not a world rule that gives equal space in every outlet. France's Law of 29 July 1881 has a rule in Article 13 for certain periodicals. The format, request, time, content, and length matter. Do not assume you must prove defamation first. A reply cannot say just anything either. Online and other media may have different rules. French rules may call for comparable placement and type. This is not a promise for every place or outlet. Keep the article and its date. Keep your exact mention, draft reply, and proof that the request arrived. Ask for legal help soon. Deadlines can be short. An editor's correction, a legal reply, and damages are different steps. General press-freedom ideas and UNESCO guidance do not replace local law. Check the current rule and facts. Do not assume refusal is unlawful or that a remedy is certain.
groups.source_review: Official Legifrance index identifies law/Article13, but full current article fetch was blocked (403). Specific deadlines and length figures deliberately not certified; current-text legal review required.
groups.notes: Corrected defamation-only framing, universal equal-space entitlement, and automatic enforcement claim. Source access limitation explicitly recorded.
